steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a cryptography/ML paper proposing a more secure and faster privacy-preserving distributed machine learning scheme based on multi-key TFHE. Explain the background on FHE and MKTFHE, the problems with non-linear functions and with the existing distributed decryption, our fixes, and list our contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Distributed ML and privacy
- FHE: single-key vs. multi-key
- MKTFHE evaluation: prior work and the non-linearity problem
- Our MKTFHE-friendly activation function with compare quads
- Decryption: distributed decryption and why it is insecure
- Our secret-sharing decryption and the SFPDML scheme
- Contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Distributed ML and privacy
  - big data era: centralized -> distributed ML systems
  - new challenges, privacy most pressing (cite)
- FHE
  - privacy computing: computation without information leakage
  - FHE for outsourcing private computations; compute on encrypted data without decrypting
  - single-key: server adds/multiplies data under same key
  - multi-key FHE (MKFHE) (cite): each user own key; decryption uses all secret keys; prevents user-server conspiracy
- MKTFHE evaluation
  - multi-key FHE over the torus, attention on evaluation + decryption
  - Chen et al.: library, evaluation of NAND gate (cite)
  - Jiang et al.: adders, subtracters, multipliers, dividers -> linear arithmetic (cite)
  - no non-linear ops (Sigmoid) -> no logistic regression / neural networks
- Our activation function
  - SecureML idea (cite): piecewise function replacing non-linear activation
  - operands -> Booleans, Boolean operations
  - piecewise hard in FHE: discontinuous, compare input with each bound
  - instead of SecureML online interactive comparison: compare quads
  - select ct_{c}/ct_{d} by comparing ct_{a}, ct_{b}: subtract, take MSB, evaluate \mathsf{MSB}\land ct_{c}+\lnot\mathsf{MSB}\land ct_{d}
  - more complex branching; SecureML-like piecewise with two compare quads
- Decryption
  - Chen et al.: naive decryption needs all secret keys (cite)
  - should be restricted in practice
  - Lee et al.: distributed decryption, partial + final decryption (cite)
  - we find possible attacks (Appendix.8)
  - partial decryption p_{i} and b leak \langle{\bf a}_{i},{\bf s}_{i}\rangle; external adversary with all p_{i} can finish final decryption
- Our decryption + scheme
  - additive secret sharing protects partial decryption, does final decryption
  - no access to others' keys (internal), no partial results (external)
  - only additions -> no interaction, similar cost
  - SFPDML: logistic regression + neural networks on Iris dataset
- Contributions
  - 1. secure distributed decryption via secret sharing; security goal vs static adversaries; correctness proof; similar performance as participants increase
  - 2. train/evaluate LR + NN; homogenizer for bit length; compare quads; 10 times faster than 7-order Taylor polynomials; similar accuracy to high-order polynomial activations

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
In the big data era, machine learning tasks need to move from centralized systems to distributed ones. But distributed systems bring new challenges, and privacy is one of the most pressing ones.

Privacy computing is a technique that lets data be computed on without any risk of information leaking. Fully homomorphic encryption (FHE), a cryptographic tool, is used to outsource private computations. FHE is a special kind of encryption that lets users do computations on encrypted data without having to decrypt it first. There are two categories of FHE: single-key fully homomorphic encryption and multi-key fully homomorphic encryption.

With single-key FHE, a server can only do addition and multiplication on data encrypted under the same key. Multi-key FHE (MKFHE), which was proposed in earlier work, lets users encrypt their own data with their own keys, but when MKFHE decrypts, the secret keys of all participants are used. This prevents a user and a server from conspiring to steal the data of other users.

In recent years multi-key fully homomorphic encryption over the torus (MKTFHE) has got a lot of attention from researchers, especially for the evaluation and decryption algorithms. Chen et al. made a library implementing MKTFHE, with an evaluation algorithm that takes a NAND gate as input. After that, Jiang et al. extended the evaluation algorithm to arithmetic operators like adders, subtracters, multipliers and dividers, so linear multi-key homomorphic arithmetic evaluation is possible in MKTFHE. But non-linear operations like the Sigmoid function still can't be evaluated, and this stops more complex machine learning schemes like logistic regression and neural networks from being applied directly.

To get past this limitation, we take the idea from SecureML of replacing the non-linear activation function with a piecewise function (an MKTFHE-friendly activation function). When the activation function is evaluated, the operands are turned into Booleans and evaluated with Boolean operations. But piecewise functions are hard to implement in FHE, because they are discontinuous and the input ciphertext has to be compared with each bound. SecureML uses an online interactive comparison, but we propose something simpler: we develop compare quads that select ciphertext ct_{c} and ct_{d} by comparing the messages of ciphertext ct_{a} and ct_{b}. We do this by subtracting ct_{a} and ct_{b}, taking the most significant bit (MSB) of the result, and using the MSB to pick the right value by homomorphically evaluating the equation \mathsf{MSB}\land ct_{c}+\lnot\mathsf{MSB}\land ct_{d}. Our compare quads support more complex branching programs, and a SecureML-like piecewise function can be implemented with only two compare quads.

- Decryption
  - Chen et al.: naive decryption, needs all users' secret keys; should be restricted in practice
  - Lee et al.: distributed decryption, partial + final decryption, each user uses own key
  - we find possible attacks (Appendix.8)
- Why previous decryption not secure
  - MKTLWE ciphertext, b=\frac{1}{4}m-\sum^{k}_{i=1}\langle{\bf a}_{i},{\bf s}_{i}\rangle+e
  - p_{i}=b+\langle{\bf a}_{i},{\bf s}_{i}\rangle minus b leaks info on {\bf s}_{i}
  - external adversary computes \sum_{i=1}^{k}p_{i}-\left(k-1\right)b
- Our fix: additive secret sharing; no interaction, similar cost
- SFPDML: logistic regression + neural networks, Iris dataset
- Contributions 1. and 2.

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
In the big data era, machine learning tasks need to move from centralized systems to distributed ones. But distributed systems bring new challenges, and privacy is one of the most pressing ones.

Privacy computing is a technique that lets data be computed on without any risk of information leaking. Fully homomorphic encryption (FHE), a cryptographic tool, is used to outsource private computations. FHE is a special kind of encryption that lets users do computations on encrypted data without having to decrypt it first. There are two categories of FHE: single-key fully homomorphic encryption and multi-key fully homomorphic encryption.

With single-key FHE, a server can only do addition and multiplication on data encrypted under the same key. Multi-key FHE (MKFHE), which was proposed in earlier work, lets users encrypt their own data with their own keys, but when MKFHE decrypts, the secret keys of all participants are used. This prevents a user and a server from conspiring to steal the data of other users.

In recent years multi-key fully homomorphic encryption over the torus (MKTFHE) has got a lot of attention from researchers, especially for the evaluation and decryption algorithms. Chen et al. made a library implementing MKTFHE, with an evaluation algorithm that takes a NAND gate as input. After that, Jiang et al. extended the evaluation algorithm to arithmetic operators like adders, subtracters, multipliers and dividers, so linear multi-key homomorphic arithmetic evaluation is possible in MKTFHE. But non-linear operations like the Sigmoid function still can't be evaluated, and this stops more complex machine learning schemes like logistic regression and neural networks from being applied directly.

To get past this limitation, we take the idea from SecureML of replacing the non-linear activation function with a piecewise function (an MKTFHE-friendly activation function). When the activation function is evaluated, the operands are turned into Booleans and evaluated with Boolean operations. But piecewise functions are hard to implement in FHE, because they are discontinuous and the input ciphertext has to be compared with each bound. SecureML uses an online interactive comparison, but we propose something simpler: we develop compare quads that select ciphertext ct_{c} and ct_{d} by comparing the messages of ciphertext ct_{a} and ct_{b}. We do this by subtracting ct_{a} and ct_{b}, taking the most significant bit (MSB) of the result, and using the MSB to pick the right value by homomorphically evaluating the equation \mathsf{MSB}\land ct_{c}+\lnot\mathsf{MSB}\land ct_{d}. Our compare quads support more complex branching programs, and a SecureML-like piecewise function can be implemented with only two compare quads.

For the decryption algorithm, Chen et al. gave a naive decryption algorithm for the original MKTFHE that takes all users' secret keys as input. In practice, access to other people's secret keys during decryption should be restricted. Lee et al. dealt with this by proposing a distributed decryption algorithm that splits decryption into two sub-algorithms, partial decryption and final decryption. Each user does partial decryption with their own secret key, so no user has access to the secret keys of others. However, we found some possible attacks on the distributed decryption algorithm, which are described in Appendix.8.

Why the previous decryption is not secure. Briefly, the existing MKTFHE scheme leaks information about user u_{i} ’s secret key s_{i} when the ciphertext and partial decryption are given. Suppose there is an MKTLWE ciphertext ({\bf a}_{1},\ldots,{\bf a}_{k},b), with b=\frac{1}{4}m-\sum^{k}_{i=1}\langle{\bf a}_{i},{\bf s}_{i}\rangle+e, where k is the number of users, m is a one-bit message, and e is an error that randomizes b. Given the partial decryption p_{i}=b+\langle{\bf a}_{i},{\bf s}_{i}\rangle and the ciphertext b, one can get \langle{\bf a}_{i},{\bf s}_{i}\rangle by subtracting them, which may leak information about {\bf s}_{i}. Also, an external adversary that gets all the partial decryption results can finish the final multi-key encryption results alone by computing \sum_{i=1}^{k}p_{i}-\left(k-1\right)b.

To fix these security problems, we introduce additive secret sharing to protect partial decryption and to do the final decryption. Each participant does partial decryption with their secret key and shares the result with the decryption parties. Then secret sharing is used to complete the final decryption, so internal adversaries can't access other people's secret keys and external adversaries can't get the partial decryption results. Only additional operations are involved, so the decryption parties don't need to interact, and our decryption protocol is secure against both internal and external adversaries and costs about the same as the original algorithm.

Finally, we put these together into our Secure and Faster Privacy-Preserving Distributed Machine Learning (SFPDML) scheme, and use it to train and predict logistic regression models and neural networks on the Iris dataset.

Our contributions are:

- 1. We develop a secure distributed decryption protocol for MKTFHE by introducing a secret sharing scheme, which solves the information leakage problem. We define our security goal for MKTFHE against possible static adversaries, then we prove the correctness and analyze the security of the protocol. Experiments show acceptable performance for the whole scheme, and similar performance to the original algorithm when the number of participants goes up.

- 2. We apply our SFPDML scheme to train and evaluate logistic regression and neural network models. We design a homogenizer that changes the bit length of operands, so fewer-bit operators can be used and operation time goes down. To implement a new MKTFHE-friendly activation function, we develop compare quads that compare and select input ciphertext. Experiments show that our function is 10 times more efficient than using 7-order Taylor polynomials directly, and the trained model's accuracy is similar to schemes with high-order polynomial activation functions.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
In the big data era, machine learning tasks increasingly need to move from centralized systems to distributed ones. However, distributed systems bring new challenges, one of the most pressing being privacy [1,2].

Privacy computing is a technique that enables data computation without risk of information leakage. To outsource private computations, fully homomorphic encryption (FHE), a cryptographic tool, is used. FHE is a special form of encryption that allows users to perform computations on encrypted data without first decrypting it. FHE can be divided into two categories: single-key fully homomorphic encryption and multi-key fully homomorphic encryption.

Single-key FHE only allows a server to perform addition and multiplication on data encrypted under the same key. In contrast, multi-key FHE (MKFHE), proposed in [3], enables users to encrypt their own data under their own keys, while the decryption of MKFHE uses all secret keys of all participants. This prevents a user and a server from conspiring to steal the data of other users.

In recent years, multi-key fully homomorphic encryption over the torus (MKTFHE) has attracted significant attention, particularly for its evaluation and decryption algorithms. Chen et al. [4] developed a library implementing MKTFHE, with an evaluation algorithm that takes a NAND gate as input. Subsequently, Jiang et al. [5] extended the evaluation algorithm to arithmetic operators such as adders, subtracters, multipliers, and dividers, enabling linear multi-key homomorphic arithmetic evaluation in MKTFHE. However, non-linear operations such as the Sigmoid function still cannot be evaluated, which prevents the direct application of more complex machine learning schemes such as logistic regression and neural networks.

To overcome this limitation, we borrow the SecureML [6] idea of replacing the non-linear activation function with a piecewise function (an MKTFHE-friendly activation function). During evaluation of the activation function, operands are transformed into Booleans and evaluated using Boolean operations. However, implementing piecewise functions in FHE is challenging because they are discontinuous and the input ciphertext must be compared with each bound. Instead of the online interactive comparison used in SecureML, we propose a simpler method: we develop compare quads that select ciphertext ct_{c} and ct_{d} by comparing the messages of ciphertext ct_{a} and ct_{b}. This is done by subtracting ct_{a} and ct_{b}, extracting the most significant bit (MSB) of the result, and using the MSB to select the appropriate value through homomorphic evaluation of the equation \mathsf{MSB}\land ct_{c}+\lnot\mathsf{MSB}\land ct_{d}. Our compare quads support more complex branching programs and allow a SecureML-like piecewise function to be implemented with only two compare quads.

Regarding the decryption algorithm, Chen et al. [4] provided a naive decryption algorithm for the original MKTFHE that requires all users' secret keys as input. In practice, access to others' secret keys during decryption should be restricted. To address this, Lee et al. [7] proposed a distributed decryption algorithm that splits decryption into two sub-algorithms: partial decryption and final decryption. Each user uses their own secret key for partial decryption, so that no user has access to others' secret keys. However, we discovered some possible attacks on the distributed decryption algorithm, described in Appendix.8.

Why the previous decryption is not secure. In brief, the existing MKTFHE scheme leaks information about user u_{i} ’s secret key s_{i} given the ciphertext and partial decryption. Suppose an MKTLWE ciphertext ({\bf a}_{1},\ldots,{\bf a}_{k},b), with b=\frac{1}{4}m-\sum^{k}_{i=1}\langle{\bf a}_{i},{\bf s}_{i}\rangle+e, k as the number of users, m as a one-bit message, and e as an error to randomize b. From the partial decryption p_{i}=b+\langle{\bf a}_{i},{\bf s}_{i}\rangle and ciphertext b, one can obtain \langle{\bf a}_{i},{\bf s}_{i}\rangle by subtraction, which may leak information about {\bf s}_{i}. Moreover, an external adversary obtaining all partial decryption results can complete the final multi-key encryption results alone by computing \sum_{i=1}^{k}p_{i}-\left(k-1\right)b.

To address these security concerns, we introduce additive secret sharing to protect partial decryption and carry out final decryption. Each participant performs partial decryption with their secret key and shares the result with the decryption parties, and secret sharing is then used to complete the final decryption. This prevents internal adversaries from accessing others' secret keys and external adversaries from obtaining partial decryption results. Since only additional operations are involved, the decryption parties do not need to interact, so our decryption protocol is secure against both internal and external adversaries at a cost similar to the original algorithm.

Finally, we combine these advances into our Secure and Faster Privacy-Preserving Distributed Machine Learning (SFPDML) scheme, which we apply to train and predict logistic regression models and neural networks on the Iris dataset.

Our contributions can be summarized as follows:

- 1. We develop a secure distributed decryption protocol for MKTFHE by introducing a secret sharing scheme, which addresses the information leakage problem. We define our security goal for MKTFHE against possible static adversaries, prove the correctness of our protocol and analyze its security. Experimental results show acceptable performance for the overall scheme, with performance similar to the original algorithm as the number of participants increases.

- 2. We apply our SFPDML scheme to train and evaluate logistic regression and neural network models. We design a homogenizer that modifies the bit length of operands, allowing fewer-bit operators to be used to reduce operation time. To implement a new MKTFHE-friendly activation function, we develop compare quads that compare and select input ciphertext. Experimental results show that our function is 10 times more efficient than using 7-order Taylor polynomials directly, and the accuracy of the trained model is similar to that of schemes with high-order polynomial activation functions.

References:
[1] Joost Verbraeken, Matthijs Wolting, Jonathan Katzy, Jeroen Kloppenburg, Tim Verbelen, and Jan S Rellermeyer. A survey on distributed machine learning. ACM Computing Surveys (CSUR) , 53(2):1–33, 2020.
[2] Qi Jia, Linke Guo, Zhanpeng Jin, and Yuguang Fang. Preserving model privacy for machine learning in distributed systems. IEEE Transactions on Parallel and Distributed Systems , 29(8):1808–1822, 2018.
[3] Adriana López-Alt, Eran Tromer, and Vinod Vaikuntanathan. On-the-fly multiparty computation on the cloud via multikey fully homomorphic encryption. In Proceedings of the 44th Symposium on Theory of Computing Conference, STOC 2012 , pages 1219–1234, 2012.
